title: The Grocery Store Survival Guide
subtitle: How to Make Practical, Blood Sugar-Conscious Choices Without Feeling Overwhelmed

pages.title: Before you shop
pages.body: A good grocery trip starts before the store. Check what you already have, choose two or three meals, and pick backup foods for busy days.
bullets: You do not need a perfect list.
A short list you use is better than an ideal list left at home.

pages.title: The five-part cart formula
pages.body: Build around vegetables, protein, fiber-rich carbohydrates, healthy fats, and flavor builders. This keeps shopping practical without depending on one brand or diet plan.
bullets: Fresh, frozen, canned, and dried foods can all fit.
Perimeter-only shopping misses many useful budget foods.

pages.title: Produce
pages.body: Choose vegetables and fruits you will actually eat. Fresh produce is wonderful, but it is not the only way to eat well.
bullets: Pre-cut vegetables can save energy.
Frozen vegetables may reduce waste.

pages.title: Frozen foods
pages.body: Frozen vegetables and fruit can be affordable, quick, and nutritious. Look for options without heavy sauces or added sugars when possible.
bullets: Frozen berries work in yogurt or oats.
Frozen greens can disappear into soups and eggs.

pages.title: Canned foods
pages.body: Canned beans, tuna, salmon, vegetables, tomato products, and soups can help on low-energy days. Rinsing canned beans or vegetables can lower sodium.
bullets: Compare labels when you can.
Keep emergency meals in the pantry.

pages.title: Protein choices
pages.body: Protein can come from eggs, fish, poultry, lean meat, tofu, tempeh, yogurt, cottage cheese, beans, lentils, nuts, and seeds.
bullets: Beans and lentils also contain carbohydrate.
Choose based on budget, culture, and medical needs.

pages.title: Beans, lentils, tofu, and plant proteins
pages.body: Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, and edamame can support filling meals. They are useful in soups, tacos, bowls, stir-fries, curries, and salads.
bullets: Seasoning matters.
Start with canned beans if dried beans feel like too much.

pages.title: Breads, grains, cereals, and tortillas
pages.body: Look for grains and breads that bring fiber and fit your glucose plan. Whole grain, serving size, and total carbohydrate are more useful than marketing claims alone.
bullets: Multigrain does not always mean whole grain.
Compare fiber and total carbohydrate.

pages.title: Dairy and alternatives
pages.body: Milk and yogurt contain carbohydrate. Plain yogurt, unsweetened fortified soy milk, and lower-sugar options may fit many plans, but allergies and preferences vary.
bullets: Check added sugar.
Choose what fits your taste and budget.

pages.title: Snacks
pages.body: A snack can be planned or it can become accidental grazing. Pair protein or fat with fiber when you want something that lasts longer.
bullets: Fruit with nuts.
Hummus with vegetables.
Yogurt with berries.

pages.title: Drinks
pages.body: Sweet drinks can add sugar quickly. Start by improving one drink you have often rather than overhauling every beverage.
bullets: Water, unsweet tea, sparkling water, or smaller sweet drinks can all be steps.
Alcohol needs medication and safety awareness.

pages.title: Reading the Nutrition Facts label
pages.body: Start with serving size, then check total carbohydrate, fiber, added sugar, saturated fat, and sodium. Percent Daily Value helps compare nutrients. [3]
bullets: 5% DV is low and 20% DV is high.
Serving size is not a personal portion prescription.

pages.title: Total carbohydrate and added sugar
pages.body: Total carbohydrate includes starches, fiber, sugars, and added sugars. Added sugars are added during processing or packaging, while naturally occurring sugars can be found in fruit and milk. [4]
bullets: Total carbohydrate matters for glucose.
Ingredient names do not replace checking total carbohydrate.

pages.title: Fiber
pages.body: Fiber can support fullness and steadier meals. The Nutrition Facts label lists dietary fiber in grams and Percent Daily Value.
bullets: Compare similar products.
Increase fiber gradually.

pages.title: Sodium
pages.body: The FDA Daily Value for sodium is less than 2,300 mg per day. Many packaged foods vary widely, so comparing labels can help. [5]
bullets: 5% DV or less is low.
20% DV or more is high.

pages.title: Ingredient lists and marketing claims
pages.body: Front labels can be useful, but they are not the whole story. Natural, keto, diabetic-friendly, low-fat, sugar-free, and no sugar added still deserve a label check.
bullets: Net carbs are not regulated the same way on every label.
Sugar-free does not always mean carbohydrate-free.

pages.title: Budget strategies
pages.body: Use store brands, frozen vegetables, canned beans, oats, eggs, lentils, rice, seasonal produce, and planned leftovers.
bullets: Shop your kitchen first.
Let budget be part of the plan, not a source of shame.

pages.title: Ten-minute meal formulas
pages.body: Fast meals can still have structure: heat a base, add protein, add vegetables, add flavor, and choose a drink.
bullets: Beans, salsa, greens, and tortillas.
Frozen vegetables, tofu, sauce, and rice.
Tuna, crackers, cucumber, fruit, and water.

pages.title: Printable grocery checklist
pages.body: Use this list as a starting point. Add what fits your family, budget, culture, and medical needs.

pages.title: Make the store easier next time
pages.body: Save one list that worked, one backup meal, and one label comparison. The next trip gets easier when you do not start from scratch.
